case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
summary: Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 does not extend to altering its basic structure. A 13-judge bench decided the case by a narrow majority, and it remains the foundation of judicial review of constitutional amendments.

case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
summary: The Court held that a law depriving a person of personal liberty under Article 21 must prescribe a procedure that is fair, just and reasonable, and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 must be read together. The case arose from the impounding of a passport without giving the holder a hearing.

case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: A Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of the death penalty for murder under Section 302 IPC. It held that death should be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases, after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

case_name: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: Applied and elaborated the rarest of rare principle from Bachan Singh in a case of multiple murders. The Court described categories, such as the manner of commission, motive and magnitude of the crime, that may justify the death penalty.

case_name: Mithu v. State of Punjab
summary: The Court struck down Section 303 IPC, which made the death sentence mandatory for a person who commits murder while serving a life sentence, as violating Articles 14 and 21. A mandatory sentence leaves no room for the court to consider the circumstances of the offence and the offender.

case_name: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: Explained when murder is made out under clause thirdly of Section 300 IPC. The prosecution must show the bodily injury, that it was intentionally inflicted, and that it was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

case_name: Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration)
summary: Arising from the conspiracy to assassinate Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, the Court examined how criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC is proved. Direct evidence of an agreement is rarely available, so conspiracy is usually inferred from the surrounding circumstances.

case_name: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar
summary: Distinguished a mere breach of contract from the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC. For cheating, the prosecution must show a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time the promise was made, not merely a later failure to perform it.

case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
summary: A Constitution Bench on anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC. It held that the power should not be hedged in with rigid conditions and that courts must exercise discretion on the facts of each case, keeping in mind Article 21.

case_name: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
summary: Issued guidelines on bail and arrest, grouping offences into categories and stressing that bail is the rule and jail the exception. It directed courts and investigating agencies to follow the procedure on arrest and avoid unnecessary detention.

case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
summary: On the misuse of Section 498A IPC, the Court directed that arrest should not be automatic in offences punishable up to seven years. Police must be satisfied that the conditions in Section 41 CrPC are met, and magistrates must check this before authorising detention.

case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
summary: Laid down mandatory guidelines for police on arrest and detention to prevent custodial torture and deaths, including preparing an arrest memo and informing a relative of the arrested person. It treated custodial violence as a violation of Article 21.

case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
summary: A Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR under Section 154 CrPC is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence. A limited preliminary inquiry is allowed only in certain categories of cases, such as matrimonial and commercial disputes.

case_name: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
summary: Held that the right to a speedy trial is part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The case exposed thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar jails who had been held longer than the maximum sentence for their alleged offences.

case_name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
summary: In the absence of a law on sexual harassment at the workplace, the Court laid down binding guidelines based on Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. These guidelines held the field until Parliament enacted a statute in 2013.

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
summary: A nine-judge bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and the freedoms in Part III. It overruled earlier decisions that had held otherwise.

case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
summary: A Constitution Bench held that Section 377 IPC is unconstitutional to the extent that it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults. The ruling relied on Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 and overruled the earlier decision in Suresh Kumar Koushal.

case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
summary: The Court struck down Section 497 IPC, the adultery provision, as unconstitutional. It held that the provision treated women as the property of their husbands and violated Articles 14, 15 and 21.

case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
summary: Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as violating the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), because its terms were vague and had a chilling effect. It upheld the blocking power under Section 69A with safeguards.

case_name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
summary: On electronic evidence, the Court held that an electronic record is admissible as secondary evidence only if the certificate required by Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act is produced.

case_name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
summary: A three-judge bench held that the Section 65B(4) certificate is a mandatory condition for admitting electronic records as secondary evidence when the original device is not produced. It reaffirmed Anvar P.V. and overruled the contrary view in Shafhi Mohammad.

case_name: Independent Thought v. Union of India
summary: Read down Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC so that sexual intercourse with a wife aged between 15 and 18 years is rape. The Court relied on the POCSO Act and the rights of the child to hold the exception arbitrary.

case_name: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India
summary: A three-judge bench upheld the main provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, including the powers of arrest, search and attachment and the twin conditions for bail in Section 45. It held that the ECIR is an internal document and need not be given to the accused.

case_name: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
summary: Held that the statutory restrictions on bail under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA do not prevent a constitutional court from granting bail where the accused has faced long incarceration and the trial is unlikely to finish soon. It relied on the right to a speedy trial under Article 21.

case_name: National Investigation Agency v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali
summary: On bail under the UAPA, the Court held that at the bail stage the court should examine the material produced by the prosecution as it stands, without weighing evidence or probing its admissibility in detail, to decide whether the accusation is prima facie true.

case_name: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
summary: Upheld the constitutional validity of Section 124A IPC (sedition) but limited it to acts that have a tendency or intention to create public disorder or incite violence. Criticism of the government that does not incite violence falls outside the section.

case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
summary: Struck down parts of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment that placed limits on judicial review and gave Directive Principles priority over Fundamental Rights. The Court held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure.

case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
summary: A nine-judge bench upheld 27 percent reservation for Other Backward Classes in central government jobs, excluded the creamy layer, and capped total reservation at 50 percent in the normal course.

case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case)
summary: After an oleum gas leak in Delhi, the Court developed the rule of absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities, without the exceptions of the Rylands v. Fletcher rule. Compensation should be linked to the size and capacity of the enterprise.

case_name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
summary: Held that the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of Indian environmental law, as elements of sustainable development. The case concerned tannery pollution in Tamil Nadu.

case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
summary: Widened the rule of locus standi, allowing any member of the public acting in good faith to approach the court on behalf of persons who cannot do so themselves. It is a foundational public interest litigation case and also dealt with the appointment and transfer of High Court judges.

case_name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
summary: An early Article 32 case in which the Court struck down a state order banning the circulation of the journal Cross Roads. It held that freedom of speech and of the press includes freedom of circulation, and that public order was not a ground for restriction under Article 19(2) as it then stood.

case_name: A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
summary: During the Emergency, a majority held that detainees could not seek habeas corpus to challenge preventive detention while the right to move the courts under Article 21 was suspended. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented, and the majority view was later disapproved in Puttaswamy.

case_name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
summary: Held that a proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, and that secularism is part of the basic structure. The Court laid down limits on when a state government can be dismissed.

case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
summary: Held that a divorced Muslim woman who cannot maintain herself is entitled to maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 CrPC, which applies irrespective of religion. Parliament later passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.

case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
summary: Held that compulsory narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests violate the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and personal liberty under Article 21. Such tests may be done only voluntarily and with safeguards.

case_name: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
summary: Held that prisoners do not lose their fundamental rights on conviction and that prison conditions are subject to review by the courts under Article 21. The Court restricted the use of solitary confinement and bar fetters.

case_name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
summary: Held that the right to livelihood is part of the right to life under Article 21, so pavement dwellers could not be evicted without a fair procedure. Eviction was allowed only after the occupants had been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

case_name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
summary: On the internet shutdown in Jammu and Kashmir, the Court held that freedom of speech and the right to carry on trade over the internet are protected under Article 19. Indefinite suspension of the internet is impermissible, and restrictions must be proportionate and published.

case_name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
summary: Upheld the constitutional validity of the criminal defamation provisions, Sections 499 and 500 IPC, holding that the right to reputation is part of Article 21 and that the provisions are reasonable restrictions on free speech.
